title: A buffered read meets the request's memory ceiling only after its last row, so one `select` holds as much of the host as its result is large while it runs.
text: `queried_rows` materializes an entire result set before anything asks the ceiling: `sqlite_rows`' `step` collects every row on a `nvs_host::blocking::run` thread, and the three wire arms append on the core until the server stops sending. The request is charged in the end — `nvs_runtime::budget::carry` moves a pool job's answer onto the caller, and the allocator publishes the overrun on the core — so the program stops with its `FATAL` and the bytes are attributed. What is not bounded is the peak: `tests/hostile/core/Db-Connection/query/01-values-that-do-not-match-and-more-rows-than-fit.nvs` step 6 builds a gigabyte of rows under a `[limits] memory` of 256M, and the process peaks near a gigabyte before it stops. A hostile case passes on how a program ends and cannot see a peak, so no proof is marked for this entry. That breaks `rule:programs/memory-priority`'s bound that memory stays under an enforceable cap, which is priority 1 rather than a footprint question. The fix is a poll inside the row loop, and it is a decision about the seam rather than about one member: none of the four `*_rows` arms is handed a `Ctx` — they take a `QueryWatch` — and the sqlite arm's loop runs on a pool thread that has no ceiling of its own, so charging it means handing the job the caller's headroom and deciding whether the poll is per row or per batch. `stream` is the member that already has the bound, because its walk returns to a statement boundary between rows.
